hypothesis.title: The Aperture of Rules
hypothesis.question: Does changing only the degrees of freedom left open by a fixed harmonic representation change perceived coherence and performer-style identity?
hypothesis.hypothesis: If a fixed eight-node harmonic path is realized through medium-aperture constraints—harmony and rhythm fixed, voicing and spacing free under a style profile—then listeners will rate it as more balanced between coherent identity and expressive surprise than either a fully fixed realization or a wide-open realization, because the medium aperture preserves the structural relations of the Tonnetz while leaving the style-bearing choices that basso continuo griffs can measure and that score representations expose unevenly across modalities.
hypothesis.rationaleMd: S1 frames harmonic materials as traversable combinatorial configurations, so a chord path can be fixed as a coherent structural variable. S2 shows that basso continuo realizations still carry measurable personal style despite strong harmonic and voice-leading conventions, suggesting that style appears in residual choices rather than total freedom. S3 shows that score understanding changes across ABC/PDF modalities and across pitch, rhythm, harmony, texture, and form levels, which supports treating representation as an aperture that opens some musical variables while narrowing others. Together, these imply a testable compositional mechanism: perceived musical agency may be strongest when the representation constrains harmonic identity but leaves style-bearing realization choices available. Disconfirming evidence would be no listener-rated difference between apertures, or a consistent preference for the narrow or wide condition under controlled mix and form.

recipe.title: Three Apertures over One Harmonic Path
recipe.bodyMd: Build one 60-second study from a fixed eight-chord path. Use S1 as the model for treating the chord sequence as a graph traversal rather than a free progression. Use S2 as the model for preserving a constrained but style-bearing realization layer. Use S3 as the warning that notation/representation determines which musical levels are easy to preserve, so document each version both as chord symbols and MIDI/staff notation. Create three renders: narrow aperture, medium aperture, and wide aperture. The expected result is that the medium aperture should preserve enough harmonic identity to feel coherent while leaving enough voicing/spacing choice to feel performed rather than mechanically fixed.

parameters.value: 8 chords, each repeated for two bars
Medium aperture varies voicing, spacing, and inner-voice motion only

dawChecklist: Create a 96 BPM session with one neutral keyboard or soft-piano instrument.
Choose an eight-chord path and freeze chord order, bar lengths, and bass rhythm for all versions.
Render Version A / narrow aperture: fixed voicing, fixed register, fixed rhythm; only velocity dynamics may vary.
Render Version B / medium aperture: fixed harmony and rhythm; vary voicing, spacing, common-tone retention, and inner-voice motion according to one consistent style profile.
Render Version C / wide aperture: preserve only the eight harmonic nodes; allow rhythm, register, voicing, and texture to vary.
Keep tempo, instrument, effects, loudness target, and total duration constant across versions.
Export A/B/C and take notes on coherence, surprise, perceived agency, and whether the harmonic path remains recognizable.

protocol.listeningContext: DAW nearfields or headphones at matched loudness
protocol.listeningMethod: Blind-shuffle A/B/C comparison after exporting all three renders
whatVaries: degrees of freedom left open by the representation
rhythmic and textural freedom in the wide-aperture condition
whatStaysConstant: bass rhythm in narrow and medium conditions
